Definition: A light-touch, hands-on manual therapy that works with the membranes and fluid around the brain and spinal cord (the craniosacral system) to release restrictions in the body.
Who it is for: Baby, child, mother, adult
What it addresses: Birth imprints held in the body, tension patterns, settling and feeding difficulty, stress after a hard birth
For the educator: in plain words: A very gentle, hands-on therapy. The practitioner uses light touch to help the body release tension, including tension from birth.
Who can practice it: Trained CST practitioner (Upledger or biodynamic craniosacral training). Often combined with a license such as massage, physical therapy, or chiropractic.
Self-help elements: Parents can learn calm, gentle holding. The therapy itself needs a trained practitioner.
Reach out if: A baby who stays tense, hard to settle, or struggles to feed after a hard birth, once the pediatrician has ruled out medical causes: a CST practitioner trained with infants.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Body tension in pregnancy, preparing the body for birth. Upledger lists conception, pregnancy, and birth among its areas.
When it fits: Birth: Support for mother and baby after a long, fast, assisted, or cesarean birth
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Settling or feeding difficulty, a baby who seems tense or startles easily
When it fits: Early childhood: Tension patterns that seem to persist from birth
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults working with their own birth story through the body
What a session looks like: Client is clothed. The practitioner rests hands lightly on the head, spine, or sacrum. A baby is often held by a parent during the session.
Questions a family might ask: Does it hurt? No, the touch is very light. Is it safe for a newborn? Choose a practitioner trained to work with infants.
How to offer it: Some families find gentle body work helpful after birth. Would you like information about craniosacral therapy?
Be careful about: Do not promise outcomes. It does not replace medical care, a feeding assessment, or a tongue-tie evaluation.
Founder or key figures: John E. Upledger (Upledger CST); Carol McLellan (CST for conception, pregnancy, and birth)
Origin: Developed by osteopathic physician John Upledger, building on Sutherland's cranial work. Upledger Institute founded 1985.
Module 12 source: Video: CranioSacral Therapy for Birth Healing and Resolution (Carol McLellan)

Definition: Ray Castellino's body-centered therapy for babies and families. It recognizes how prenatal and birth trauma is imprinted in the body and supports its resolution through a seven-step process.
Who it is for: Newborn, baby, whole family
What it addresses: Prenatal and birth trauma held in the body, early overwhelm, interrupted bonding
For the educator: in plain words: A body-centered way of being with babies and families. It slows down, follows the baby's cues, and helps the baby's birth story be seen and resolved.
Who can practice it: Practitioners trained in Castellino's prenatal and birth therapy
Self-help elements: Parents can slow down, watch the baby's cues, and speak to the baby about what happened.
Reach out if: A baby who startles often, cries without settling, or struggles to attach at the breast, or parents who feel the birth is still with them: a practitioner trained in Castellino's prenatal and birth therapy.
Find a practitioner: Search: Castellino Prenatal and Birth Therapy training (not verified) | APPPAH Practitioner Directory
When it fits: Birth: A baby who shows signs of overwhelm after birth
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Signs Castellino describes: a startle (Moro) response to sound or movement, crying that does not settle, trouble attaching at the breast
When it fits: Early childhood: Behaviors or struggles that may trace back to the womb or birth
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults resolving their own prenatal and birth imprints
What a session looks like: A family session with the baby present. The pace is slow. The practitioner watches the baby's movements and supports parents and baby together.
Questions a family might ask: Can a baby remember birth? Castellino holds that babies carry their birth experience in body and behavior.
How to offer it: Babies often tell their birth story through their bodies. Some practitioners specialize in helping families listen.
Be careful about: Castellino's statements, such as how widespread birth trauma is and his catecholamine hypothesis, are his clinical views.
Origin: Introduced Somatotropic Therapy in 1996, within prenatal and perinatal psychology
Module 12 source: Article: Being with Newborns: An Introduction to Somatotropic Therapy (Castellino)

Definition: A psychotherapy approach for infants, children, and adults that treats prenatal and birth trauma through regression, emotional release, and empathic response from parents and practitioner.
Who it is for: Infant, child, adult
What it addresses: Birth trauma, including cesarean birth: feeling stuck, giving up, feeling intruded upon, rescue fantasies
For the educator: in plain words: A therapy that helps babies and children express a hard birth while parents respond with empathy, so trust and bonding can grow.
Who can practice it: Therapist trained in Emerson's methods
Self-help elements: Parents can meet crying with empathy and acknowledge the baby's experience.
Reach out if: After a cesarean or difficult birth, a baby or child who seems stuck, distressed, or hard to comfort: a therapist trained in Emerson's methods.
Find a practitioner: emersonbirthrx.com (from module notes, directory not verified)
When it fits: Birth: After a cesarean or difficult birth
When it fits: Fourth trimester: A baby who seems distressed after a hard or cesarean birth
When it fits: Early childhood: Children who feel stuck in transitions, give up easily, or feel misunderstood
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults working with their own birth through regression
What a session looks like: Parent present. The baby is invited to the edge of a memory and may cry or push, and the therapist and parent respond with empathy. Five conditions: catharsis, empathy, empowerment, choice, boundaries.
Questions a family might ask: Will this upset my baby? Babies are given choice, and treatment stops when they signal no.
How to offer it: Some families find it helpful to work with a hard birth early, with a specialist who includes the parents.
Be careful about: Based mostly on Emerson's own case studies. Reading crying as memory is his interpretation.
Origin: First in the field to develop treatment for infants with prenatal and perinatal trauma. Published in JOPPPAH, 2001.
Module 12 source: Article: Treating Cesarean Birth Trauma During Infancy and Childhood (Emerson)

Definition: Approaches that help babies release birth patterns through movement, touch, and attuned interaction, usually with parents taking part.
Who it is for: Baby and parents
What it addresses: Birth patterns showing in posture and movement, tension, settling
For the educator: in plain words: Gentle movement, baby yoga, and tummy time with parents, to help babies move through birth patterns toward easy, natural movement.
Who can practice it: Trained practitioners (GoGo Babies, integrative baby therapy). Some parts are safe for parents to learn.
Self-help elements: Tummy time, floor play, gentle movement, responsive holding
Reach out if: A baby who arches, favors one side, or seems uncomfortable moving: the pediatrician first, then a trained baby therapist.
When it fits: Fourth trimester: A baby who arches, prefers one side, or seems uncomfortable in some positions
When it fits: Early childhood: Movement or settling patterns parents want support with
What a session looks like: Parent and baby together on the floor, with guided movement and play
Questions a family might ask: Is this the same as physical therapy? No, it is a gentle, relational approach. Developmental concerns go to the pediatrician.
How to offer it: Would you like some gentle movement ideas for you and your baby, and a practitioner who teaches them?
Be careful about: Developmental concerns go to the pediatrician first.
Founder or key figures: Ellynne Skove (GoGo Babies); Matthew Appleton (integrative baby therapy)
Origin: Skove: creative arts and somatic PPN therapy. Appleton: body psychotherapy and craniosacral therapy.
Module 12 source: Videos: Healing and Resolving: Babies Repatterning their Birth Imprints (Skove); Recognising Birth Trauma Behaviours (Appleton)

Definition: Skin-to-skin contact between parent and baby, from birth and as continuously as possible, with breast milk and support for the parent and baby together.
Who it is for: Preterm and full-term newborn, mother, father or partner
What it addresses: Regulation, bonding, breastfeeding, temperature and cardiorespiratory stability, neurodevelopment, pain
For the educator: in plain words: Holding your baby skin to skin on your bare chest. It helps your baby's body settle and supports bonding and feeding.
Who can practice it: Parents do it. In the NICU it is guided by the care team.
Self-help elements: Yes. A core practice for parents.
Reach out if: Any concern about a baby's breathing, color, or temperature during skin to skin, or a preterm or medically fragile baby: the NICU or care team right away.
Find a practitioner: Hospital or NICU care team | kangaroomothercare.com (Bergman)
When it fits: Pregnancy: Plan for skin to skin right after birth
When it fits: Birth: Skin to skin in the first hour
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Daily skin to skin. A partner can do it too.
What a session looks like: Baby in a diaper on a parent's bare chest, covered, for long stretches
Questions a family might ask: Can my partner do it? Yes. Is it safe in the NICU? The care team guides it for each baby.
How to offer it: Skin to skin helps babies settle. Would you like to plan for it?
Be careful about: Medically fragile babies need NICU guidance. Teach safe positioning and staying awake while holding.
Origin: Developed for preterm infants. The Canadian Paediatric Society recommends it for all nurseries caring for preterm infants.
Module 12 source: Articles: Kangaroo care for the preterm infant and family; Stanford Medicine skin-to-skin study

Definition: Clinical hypnosis combined with regression to find the origin of a fear or belief, including in the womb or at birth.
Who it is for: Child, adult
What it addresses: Anxiety and fear rooted in prenatal or birth experiences, twin loss in the womb
For the educator: in plain words: A guided, deeply relaxed state that helps a person find where a fear began. Ingram finds that knowing the origin opens the way to healing.
Who can practice it: Licensed therapist or certified hypnotherapist with regression training
Self-help elements: Limited: relaxation and noticing feelings. The regression itself is guided.
Reach out if: A fear of birth or lifelong anxiety that feels older than this pregnancy and does not ease with self-care: a licensed therapist or certified hypnotherapist with regression training.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Fear of birth that seems older than the pregnancy
When it fits: Adulthood: Lifelong anxiety without a clear cause; guilt or longing that may link to a lost twin
What a session looks like: Conversation, then a hypnotic induction, then guided regression toward the origin of a feeling
Questions a family might ask: Will I lose control? In hypnosis the person stays aware and can stop.
How to offer it: If a fear feels older than this pregnancy, some therapists help people look for where it began.
Be careful about: Ingram also works with past lives. Present that as her framework. Very early memories in hypnosis can be distorted.
Origin: Psychotherapist and hypnotherapist with over 35 years of practice. Author of Born Scared.
Module 12 source: Article: Hypnotherapy in the Treatment of Children and Adults Who Suffer Anxiety Due to Prenatal and Birth Trauma (Ingram)

Definition: A hypnoanalytic therapy that works with ego states, parts of the personality that form naturally or split off during trauma.
Who it is for: Pregnant person deciding about an abortion; adults who survived an attempted abortion
What it addresses: Guilt and grief around abortion; an early sense of not being wanted
For the educator: in plain words: A therapy that uses hypnosis and visualization to work with feelings and parts of the self, including speaking with the baby.
Who can practice it: Licensed therapist trained in ego-state therapy and clinical hypnosis
Self-help elements: Quiet breathing, a hand on the belly, speaking to the baby. In the article this was done alongside therapy.
Reach out if: Guilt or grief around a pregnancy decision or loss, or a lifelong sense of not being wanted: a licensed therapist trained in ego-state therapy or clinical hypnosis.
Find a practitioner: Not verified. Look for a licensed therapist trained in ego-state therapy or clinical hypnosis.
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults with a lifelong sense of not being wanted. Grief after a past abortion is not covered in the article, though the approach may apply.
What a session looks like: Hypnotic induction, visualizing the baby, silent dialogue. The affect bridge follows a feeling back to where it began.
Questions a family might ask: Is this only for abortion? No. Ego-state therapy is used for many kinds of early trauma.
How to offer it: Some therapists help people work through grief or guilt around a pregnancy decision. Would you like a referral?
Be careful about: 1986 case reports. The article does not address healing after an abortion has already happened. Leave out its miscarriage anecdotes.
Founder or key figures: Helen H. Watkins and John G. Watkins
Origin: Co-creators of Ego State Therapy, University of Montana
Module 12 source: Article: Treating the Trauma of Abortion (Watkins, 1986)

Definition: Therapeutic hypnosis combined with body awareness and inner child work to access and heal early memories.
Who it is for: Adult
What it addresses: Early imprints and unresolved wounds that shape adult behavior, health, and relationships
For the educator: in plain words: A guided practice that uses body awareness and hypnosis to meet the younger self and heal early memories.
Who can practice it: Trained hypnotherapist
Self-help elements: Body awareness and inner child reflection
Reach out if: Early memories or old wounds that keep shaping daily life and relationships: a trained hypnotherapist, or a licensed therapist if distress is strong.
What a session looks like: Somatic awareness exercises, then therapeutic hypnosis
Questions a family might ask: What is an inner child? The younger self who still carries early feelings.
How to offer it: Some people find it healing to revisit their earliest experiences with a trained guide.
Be careful about: The quiz describes three kinds of memory (historical, emotional, decision). Not verified against the source.
Origin: Co-founder of Birth the Change and Birthing the New Humanity; hypnotherapy trainer
Module 12 source: Video: How to Access Early Memories and Change Your Life (Gerland)

Definition: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing: an eight-phase psychotherapy that uses side-to-side stimulation (eye movements, taps, or tones) to help reprocess disturbing memories.
Who it is for: Adult; child with a child-trained therapist
What it addresses: Trauma memories, including prenatal and perinatal trauma and a mother's traumatic birth
For the educator: in plain words: A structured therapy that uses eye movements or other side-to-side stimulation to help the brain reprocess hard memories so they feel less charged.
Who can practice it: Licensed mental health professional with EMDR training
Self-help elements: No. Done with a trained therapist.
Reach out if: Flashbacks, nightmares, panic, or avoidance after a traumatic birth or early trauma: a licensed therapist trained in EMDR.
When it fits: Birth: A mother's distress after a traumatic birth
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Postpartum distress linked to the birth
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults with prenatal or perinatal trauma
What a session looks like: Eight phases: choosing a memory, naming negative and positive beliefs, sets of eye movements, body scan, and installing the positive belief
Questions a family might ask: What are the eye movements for? They help the brain process a memory while the person stays in the present.
How to offer it: There is a well-established therapy for traumatic memories, including a hard birth. Would you like a referral?
Be careful about: Prenatal and transpersonal use in MacLean's article is case-based. EMDR for trauma in general has a broad research base.
Origin: Shapiro describes it as integrating psychodynamic, experiential, behavioral, cognitive, body-based, and systems therapies.
Module 12 source: Article: Transpersonal Dimensions in Healing Pre/Perinatal Trauma with EMDR (MacLean)

Definition: A psycho-sensory technique that pairs soothing touch with attention exercises to reduce the emotional charge of distressing memories.
Who it is for: Adult, pregnant or postpartum mother, child
What it addresses: Distressing memories and emotions, stress, building calm and resilience
For the educator: in plain words: A gentle touch technique, stroking the arms, face, and palms, that calms the nervous system while working with a hard feeling.
Who can practice it: Certified Havening Techniques practitioner. Self-havening can be taught.
Self-help elements: Yes: self-havening touch for calm
Reach out if: Self-havening does not settle the feeling, or strong emotions surface during practice: a certified Havening practitioner.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Stress, anxiety, or fear in pregnancy
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Postpartum overwhelm or distress after birth
What a session looks like: Rate the distress, apply havening touch with a distraction or imagery, rate again. Touch only with consent, and clients can apply it themselves.
Questions a family might ask: Can I do this on my own? Yes, self-havening is often taught. A practitioner is best for deeper trauma.
How to offer it: Here is a simple calming touch you can try, and there are practitioners if you want to go deeper.
Be careful about: Deeper trauma needs a certified practitioner, since strong emotions can surface.
Founder or key figures: Ronald Ruden, MD (founder); Alison Shaloe and Ellynne Skove (module presenters)
Origin: Developed by Ronald Ruden. Havening Techniques is a registered trademark.
Module 12 source: Video: An Introduction to Havening (Shaloe and Skove)

Definition: Often called tapping: tapping on acupressure points while focusing on a problem or feeling, to reduce emotional distress.
Who it is for: Adult, pregnant or postpartum mother, older child
What it addresses: Stress, fear, the emotional charge of memories, fear of birth
For the educator: in plain words: Tapping lightly on points on the face and body while naming a feeling, to calm it.
Who can practice it: Self-use is common. For trauma, a trained EFT practitioner.
Self-help elements: Yes: basic tapping
Reach out if: Tapping brings up strong distress, or the issue is a significant trauma: a trained EFT practitioner or licensed therapist.
Find a practitioner: Not verified. Look for an accredited EFT practitioner.
What a session looks like: Name the issue, rate its intensity, tap through the points while speaking, rate again
Questions a family might ask: Why tap? Tapping while naming a feeling seems to help the body settle.
How to offer it: Here is a simple tapping practice for stress. A practitioner can help with bigger things.
Be careful about: Strong trauma needs a trained practitioner.
Origin: Created by Gary Craig. The basis for Matrix Reimprinting.
Module 12 source: Required reading: King, Heal Your Birth Heal Your Life

Definition: A protocol that combines EFT tapping with imagery to revisit one's own conception, womb, or birth experience, or one's experience of giving birth, and reimprint it with a more supportive version.
Who it is for: Adult (own birth), mother (her birth experience), parent with child
What it addresses: Imprints and beliefs from conception, pregnancy, and birth; a birth experience a mother wants to transform
For the educator: in plain words: Using tapping and imagination, a person revisits their birth or birthing experience and rewrites it with the support and bonding that was missing.
Who can practice it: Trained Matrix Birth Reimprinting (Heal Your Birth) practitioner
Self-help elements: Some. The book offers self-help tools, but King advises a practitioner for significant trauma.
Reach out if: A birth experience that still feels heavy or traumatic: a trained Matrix Birth ReImprinting practitioner, as King advises for significant trauma.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Easing fears, or a previous birth, before this one
When it fits: Fourth trimester: A mother healing her birth experience
What a session looks like: Tapping while in the memory, imagining tapping on the younger self, creating a new picture
Questions a family might ask: Does this change what happened? No. It changes how the experience is held now.
How to offer it: Some mothers find it healing to revisit their birth with support and give it a new ending.
Be careful about: King cautions that significant trauma needs a practitioner. Based on a theory of a connecting energy field.
Origin: Built on Karl Dawson's Matrix Reimprinting and Gary Craig's EFT. Now called Heal Your Birth.
Module 12 source: Required reading: King, Heal Your Birth Heal Your Life

Definition: A consciousness-based energy approach that uses muscle feedback to find priorities and tapping to restore communication between the body's systems.
Who it is for: Whole family: pregnant and postpartum person, newborn, other children
What it addresses: Stress and the balance of body systems, early imprints
For the educator: in plain words: An energy-based approach that uses light tapping on the head and chest to help the body's systems communicate and rebalance.
Who can practice it: Certified BodyTalk practitioner. The Cortices technique is taught to the public.
Self-help elements: Yes: Cortices tapping across the three brains (head, heart, gut)
Reach out if: Stress or imbalance that continues after simple tapping practices: a certified BodyTalk practitioner, alongside medical care for any health concern.
What a session looks like: The practitioner uses muscle feedback, then taps on the head and sternum. The client stays clothed.
Questions a family might ask: Is it like acupuncture? It draws on energy medicine, but there are no needles.
How to offer it: Here is a short tapping practice some families use for calm.
Be careful about: Consciousness-based, with little scientific research. Present it as complementary.
Founder or key figures: John Veltheim; Phyllis Klaus and Joann Fisher (module presenters)
Origin: Developed in the 1990s by John Veltheim, an Australian chiropractor and acupuncturist. International BodyTalk Association founded 2000.
Module 12 source: Video: How Prenatal and Perinatal Experiences Reverberate Throughout a Person's Life (Klaus and Fisher)

Definition: A method of regular sessions from mid-pregnancy that supports bonding and two-way communication between mother and unborn baby. Also called Bonding Analysis (Bindungsanalyse).
Who it is for: Pregnant mother, prenate, partner
What it addresses: Bonding and communication with the unborn baby; preparing for birth and postpartum
For the educator: in plain words: A guided series of sessions in pregnancy that helps the mother connect and communicate with her baby.
Who can practice it: Certified Prenatal Bonding (BA) facilitator
Self-help elements: Talking to the baby, resting attention on the womb
Reach out if: A mother who struggles to feel connected to her baby, or a pregnancy after loss: a certified Prenatal Bonding (BA) facilitator. Persistent low mood or anxiety: a perinatal mental health provider.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Begins around week 20 and continues until birth
When it fits: Birth: Mother and baby come to birth already in relationship
When it fits: Fourth trimester: The postpartum becomes a continuation of an established relationship
What a session looks like: Regular sessions with relaxation, as the mother turns her attention to the womb and baby
Questions a family might ask: When can we start? Around the 20th week of pregnancy.
How to offer it: Some parents enjoy a guided practice for connecting with their baby before birth.
Be careful about: Outcome figures come from a retrospective study by practitioners who also teach the method.
Founder or key figures: Jeno Raffai and Gyorgy Hidas; Gerhard Schroth and Anne Goertz-Schroth
Origin: Developed in Hungary in the early 1990s (Bindungsanalyse)
Module 12 source: Video: Prenatal Bonding (BA): What, When, How, and Why (Barbara Decker)

Definition: A Heartfulness meditation practice that uses relaxation, attention to the womb, and intention to clear impressions (samskaras) from the womb space.
Who it is for: Couples preparing to conceive, pregnant mother
What it addresses: Clearing impressions from the womb space, calm, intention for conception
For the educator: in plain words: A guided meditation where the mother rests attention on her womb, lets go of what feels heavy, and sets an intention for her baby.
Who can practice it: Self-practice. Heartfulness trainers guide programs.
Self-help elements: Yes
Reach out if: Old grief, a previous loss, or heaviness that meditation stirs up: a Heartfulness trainer for guidance, or a licensed therapist for grief or trauma.
When it fits: Preconception: Divya Janani, a 12-week program for couples preparing to conceive
What a session looks like: Relaxation, attention to the heart and womb, imagining heaviness leaving as smoke, an intention
Questions a family might ask: Is it religious? It comes from a meditation tradition and can be done as a quiet practice.
How to offer it: Here is a meditation some mothers use to feel close to their womb and baby.
Be careful about: Spiritual framework. Offer it as a contemplative practice.
Origin: Heartfulness, a heart-centered meditation tradition
Module 12 source: Womb Cleaning slides and video (Heartfulness)

Definition: The use of voice, singing, music, chanting, toning, and sound therapy to calm the nervous system and support bonding and health.
Who it is for: Fetus, newborn, preterm infant, mother, child
What it addresses: The stress response, regulation, bonding, voice tones
For the educator: in plain words: Using the mother's voice, singing, lullabies, and gentle music to calm and connect with the baby.
Who can practice it: Self-practice. A board-certified music therapist in the NICU. Sound healers.
Self-help elements: Yes: singing, talking, lullabies
Reach out if: A baby in the NICU: ask the care team about a board-certified music therapist.
Find a practitioner: Not verified. Ask the hospital about music therapy.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Talking and singing to the baby
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Lullabies, the mother's voice, NICU music
What a session looks like: Mother sings or talks to the baby. Recordings of her voice may be used in the NICU.
Questions a family might ask: Does it matter if I cannot sing? No. Newborns prefer their own mother's voice.
How to offer it: Your voice is familiar to your baby. Singing or talking can be calming for you both.
Be careful about: Claims about voice tones and health are practice-based.
Founder or key figures: Fred J. Schwartz, MD; Ani Williams
Origin: Schwartz: anesthesiologist and music therapist. Williams: harpist, singer, and sound healer.
Module 12 source: Articles: Music for Babies (Schwartz); Music for Infants and Children; Sound Healing (Williams)

Definition: A clinical hypnosis method that helps a mother repair an early break in the bond with her child. Madrid studied it in relation to childhood asthma.
Who it is for: Mother and child of any age
What it addresses: An interrupted mother-child bond, such as separation at birth; links Madrid found with childhood asthma
For the educator: in plain words: A therapy that uses clinical hypnosis to help heal the bond between a mother and her child.
Who can practice it: Licensed therapist trained in clinical hypnosis
Self-help elements: Limited
Reach out if: A separation at birth or NICU stay that still feels unresolved, or a child with asthma or bonding difficulty (alongside medical care): a therapist trained in Bonding Repair Therapy or clinical hypnosis.
When it fits: Early childhood: A child with asthma or bonding difficulty
What a session looks like: The mother works in hypnosis with the bond to her child (see the Madrid article for details)
Questions a family might ask: Is it too late to repair a bond? Madrid's work suggests repair is possible later.
How to offer it: If a separation early on still feels unresolved, there is therapy that focuses on repairing that bond.
Be careful about: The asthma link is Madrid's research. It does not replace asthma care.
Origin: Clinical hypnosis, EMDR, and maternal-infant bonding work
Module 12 source: Video and article: Bonding Repair Therapy and Asthma (Madrid)

Definition: Somatic psychotherapy, drawing on Body-Mind Centering, that uses body awareness and movement to resolve birth trauma.
Who it is for: Parents, children, adults
What it addresses: Birth trauma held in the body
For the educator: in plain words: Body-based awareness and movement that helps the body complete and release birth experiences.
Who can practice it: Somatic psychotherapist
Self-help elements: Some somatic practices
Reach out if: Birth experiences that seem held in the body and do not ease with gentle self-care: a somatic psychotherapist.
When it fits: Early childhood: Children who seem to carry birth patterns
What a session looks like: Somatic exercises and guided awareness
Questions a family might ask: What does somatic mean? Working through the body, not only through talk.
How to offer it: Some people heal birth experiences through gentle body-based work.
Be careful about: Present as complementary to medical and mental health care.
Origin: Founder of the Brook Institute, with a background in Body-Mind Centering
Module 12 source: Video: Helping Parents, Children, and Adults Heal from Birth Trauma (Brook)

Definition: An integrative prenatal and perinatal approach that includes the baby directly as a conscious participant, uses energy psychology tools, and supports wholeness and human potential from the beginning of life.
Who it is for: Baby, parents, whole family
What it addresses: Healing early trauma and unmet needs, and supporting optimal development, wholeness, and human potential
For the educator: in plain words: Treating the baby as a full participant, and helping families speak honestly and lovingly about what happened in the womb and at birth.
Who can practice it: Practitioners trained in prenatal and perinatal psychology
Self-help elements: Yes: telling a child the genuine, caring story of their birth
Reach out if: Families who want help telling a hard birth story or including their baby in healing: a practitioner trained in prenatal and perinatal psychology.
Find a practitioner: wondrousbeginnings.com (from module notes) | APPPAH Practitioner Directory
When it fits: Pregnancy: Conscious pregnancy and speaking with the baby
When it fits: Fourth trimester: Speaking to the baby about what is happening
When it fits: Early childhood: Telling the child the genuine story of their birth
When it fits: Adulthood: Adults exploring their own earliest experiences
What a session looks like: Family sessions that include the baby directly, using energy psychology tools
Questions a family might ask: Should I tell my child about a hard birth? McCarty describes healing in telling the genuine story, with care and at the child's level.
How to offer it: Many parents find it healing to tell their child the real story of their beginning, gently.
Be careful about: Grounded in a view of babies as conscious beings. Much of it rests on clinical experience.
Origin: Nurse and psychologist; founding chair and core faculty at Santa Barbara Graduate Institute; author of Welcoming Consciousness
Module 12 source: Interview with Dr. Wendy Anne McCarty (Kate White)

Definition: Prenatal bonding and womb practices that blend Western somatic and prenatal and perinatal psychology with Eastern spiritual healing traditions, offered to the whole family.
Who it is for: Pregnant mother, babies, whole family
What it addresses: Healing past trauma at any age, soul-to-soul connection in the family, helping babies stay connected to themselves
For the educator: in plain words: Practices that nurture the womb as the baby's first home and deepen the connection between mother, baby, and family.
Who can practice it: Practitioner trained in somatic and prenatal psychology
Self-help elements: Some practices the family can do together
Reach out if: Past trauma that surfaces through womb or family practices: a practitioner trained in somatic and prenatal psychology, or a licensed therapist.
When it fits: Pregnancy: Nurturing the womb environment and bonding
When it fits: Adulthood: Healing past traumas through family connection
What a session looks like: Wisdom practices and somatic work, in person or online
Questions a family might ask: Is this religious? It draws on spiritual traditions and can be offered as a contemplative practice.
How to offer it: Some families enjoy practices that honor the womb as the baby's first home.
Be careful about: The claim that these practices are over 7,000 years old is the presenter's. Offer as contemplative and spiritual practice.
Origin: Clinical psychology with a somatic specialty; PPNE graduate and mentor; studied at Sri Kaleshwar's Soul University in India
Module 12 source: Video: The Mother's Womb: Wisdom for Prenatal Bonding (Ketscher)
